title: The resolve that opens a puja
hook: before a puja, the priest names the age of the world and the family's name, then begins
carry: sankalpa: my small act, placed in God's time

segments.voice: Yesterday, yoga nidra with Patanjali: too much sleep is tamas, not yoga.

Sunday morning at a grandmother's house, smelling of ghee and marigolds. A priest sits cross-legged before a small altar, and before a single flower is offered, he asks a question. Your name? Your gotra, your family line? Then he takes a little water in his right hand and starts reciting, quickly, in Sanskrit: a long string about the second half of Brahma's life, the age of the White Boar, the Kali Yuga, this land, this day. Only then does the puja begin.
screen: `GHEE AND MARIGOLDS.` → `YOUR NAME? YOUR GOTRA?` → `THE AGE OF THE WORLD, THEN TODAY'S DATE.`

segments.voice: That recitation is the sankalpa, the resolve, and in a common form it begins with the whole of time. The second half of Brahma's life. The kalpa, the cosmic day, called Shveta Varaha, the White Boar. That name carries a story. The Bhagavata Purana tells that the earth once sank deep into the cosmic waters, and Brahma, just beginning to make the world, didn't know how to bring her back. Then from his nostril came a tiny boar, no bigger than a thumb. It grew, and grew, until it filled the sky. It was Vishnu. He dove into the flood, found the earth at the bottom, and lifted her up on his tusks while the sages sang his praise. Our cosmic day carries the name of that rescue. Then it zooms in: this age, the Kali Yuga; this land; this year, month and day; this person, this family line; and this purpose. Here's the teaching: in Hindu worship, an offering isn't tossed off. Before you act, you say who you are, where you stand in God's vast time, and why you're doing it. Then you offer it. A single flower becomes a deliberate act, set inside a story as old as the earth's rescue. That's why the word turned up in the mantra days, and why yoga nidra borrowed it. Swami Satyananda of the Bihar School, who set out the guided form, opens and closes the practice with a sankalpa: short, sincere, at the start and again near the end. Rest, like worship, begins on purpose.
screen: `SANKALPA: THE RESOLVE THAT OPENS A PUJA.` · `OUR COSMIC DAY: THE WHITE BOAR.` · `VISHNU LIFTS THE EARTH ON HIS TUSKS.` · `THE AGE, THE PLACE, THE DAY, THE PERSON, THE PURPOSE.` · then, large: `MY SMALL ACT, PLACED IN GOD'S TIME.`

segments.voice: Sit up for a moment. If you pray, cup a little water in your right hand, or simply cup the hand, and make a tiny sankalpa in your own words: who you are, today's date, where you are, and what you offer this rest for; then let the water go, or open the hand. If you don't pray, say it as a quiet promise. Now lie back, hear the far sounds, the near ones, the breath, and rest. Near the end, say your sankalpa once more.
Yoga nidra. The sleep of yoga, which in its guided form opens and closes with a sankalpa, the same resolve that opens a puja.
Your line: sankalpa, my small act, placed in God's time. The White Boar's day, and yours. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Before a puja or a vrata, the priest or householder makes a sankalpa, often holding water in the right hand, naming the age of the world, the place, the date, the person and family line, and the purpose; guided yoga nidra opens and closes with a short sankalpa of the practitioner's own.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: sankalpa, resolve, intention. Made before a puja, and at the start and end of yoga nidra.

trapdoor: what you thought: the priest's long opening is just formalities.

what a scholar hears: the puja sankalpa (dvitiya parardhe, shveta varaha kalpe, vaivasvata manvantare, kali yuge), Bhagavata Purana 3.13, and Satyananda's yoga nidra.

notes: Editor pass: review updated for 1022's new carry; the claim that studio yoga nidra 'today owes its shape' to Satyananda narrowed to what his own book says; sankalpa now acknowledged as met at the start of the mantra block (1012) instead of introduced as new; puja sankalpa 'often' softened to 'may'.

Attribution of the modern guided form to Swami Satyananda Saraswati and the Bihar School, and the link to older tantric practices (nyasa), is a historical claim not from a scripture; confirm wording. His book is under copyright and is only paraphrased; no dates are given on purpose.
The outline (shavasana, sankalpa, rotation of consciousness, breath, opposites, visualization, sankalpa, ending) is summarized from Satyananda's teaching; confirm order.
Satyananda's advice on the sankalpa (short, positive, repeated three times at start and end, said when the mind is receptive) is paraphrased; confirm.
The puja sankalpa (naming time, place, person, purpose) is described generally; customs vary by region and lineage.
The hook's 'a dozen people' is a scene detail, not a statistic.
Audit: removed 'then, he says, let it go, and don't keep checking on it' (teach and fork reveal); that advice could not be confirmed as Satyananda's and was attributed to him directly.
Restyled 2026-10-07 (job 2): voice tightened; content and sources unchanged.
2026-10-07 (job 3): new recipe data added (chat, gloss, recall); confirm the chat reply, glosses, scripts and pronunciations with the Keeper.

2026-10-15 quality pass: rewritten: the day had no story and its carry ('a short, sincere resolve') was a self-help line. Now the puja sankalpa is the scene, its naming of our kalpa as Shveta Varaha carries the Varaha story (Bhagavata 3.13: the thumb-sized boar from Brahma's nostril grows, dives, lifts the earth on his tusks), and the teaching is named plainly: a Hindu act of worship is placed on purpose inside God's time (age, place, date, person, family line, purpose); yoga nidra's sankalpa (Satyananda) follows from it. Title and carry now real; practice is a tiny sankalpa with water or open hand (a promise if you don't pray); games test the sankalpa and the story; chat moved to Priya (Nani's puja, the pandit asks her gotra) with a tie; shavasana gloss dropped, Varaha and gotra added; sources add Bhagavata 3.13 and the puja sankalpa. Keeper: confirm the sankalpa outline (dvitiya parardhe, shveta varaha kalpe, kali yuge, place, date, gotra, name, purpose) and the water-in-the-right-hand custom as fair general descriptions; the older note about 'a dozen people' in the hook is stale.

2026-10-15 quality pass: second editor checked the Varaha story against Bhagavata 3.13 (thumb-sized boar from Brahma's nostril, lifts the earth on his tusks) and the common sankalpa outline; one line softened so the sankalpa is not said to explain the kalpa's name itself. Title, carry, chat and tie kept.
